article.overview: A laser altimeter fires short pulses of laser light at a surface and measures how long each pulse takes to return. Light travels at a known speed, so the round-trip time gives the distance from the instrument to the ground. Repeated along the track of a spacecraft, these distance measurements form topographic profiles that can be combined into maps of surface height. The catalogue entry 47 (Laser altimeter) is a class name, so this article describes several flown and documented instruments rather than one design. In scope: pulsed-laser instruments whose documented function includes measuring surface height or range to the surface, from orbit or from a lander. The examples are the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter [1][2][3]; the Laser Altimeter (LALT) on Japan's KAGUYA (SELENE) orbiter [5]; the Lunar Laser Ranging Instrument (LLRI) on India's Chandrayaan-1 orbiter [9]; the altimeter mode of the imaging lidar on the Clementine spacecraft [6]; and the Laser Altimeter (LAM) on China's Chang'e-1 orbiter [7]. Status is stated per example. LOLA, LALT, LLRI, the Clementine lidar and the Chang'e-1 LAM are all described in the sources as flown on lunar missions. LOLA's current operating status was not confirmed beyond the most recent primary paper accessed, which describes operations to 2016 [1]. The LOLA pre-launch fact sheet is a design document, not a flight measurement [3]. No flight-qualified-but-unflown or proposed laser altimeter was verified in this run, so none is described as an example. Neighbouring entries are covered elsewhere and are not repeated here. Imaging lidar scanners are in 046 (Lidar scanner). Dedicated laser rangefinders are in 048 (Laser rangefinder). Surface height products from stereo imagery are in 028 (Terrain mapping camera) and 050 (Digital terrain mapping system). Topography products as a category are in 051 (Surface topography mapper). Chandrayaan-3's lander carried a laser altimeter listed by ISRO, but its specifications were not verified in this run, so it is noted in the Limitations section only. A Navigation Doppler Lidar flown on Intuitive Machines' IM-1 lander is an adjacent laser ranging and velocity sensor [11]. It is noted but not profiled here because its primary function is navigation, and it overlaps with 046 and 048.
article.description: A laser altimeter is a ranging instrument. Its laser transmitter emits a short pulse, a telescope collects the reflected light, and a detector records the time at which the pulse returns. The LOLA design illustrates the main parts. A laser transmitter sends a pulse through a diffractive optical element, which splits it into five beams arranged in a cross pattern [2][3]. A receiver telescope with a 14 cm aperture collects the returns, and five silicon avalanche photodiodes detect them [3][2]. Each beam gives three measurements: the range, the spread of the returning pulse (related to surface roughness), and the returned energy (related to surface reflectance) [1]. The five-beam pattern also lets LOLA estimate slopes in along-track and cross-track directions [3]. Earlier and later designs differ. The Clementine lidar, for example, made single-spot ranging measurements and also worked as an imaging lidar [6].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
- Global topography and a geodetic reference. LOLA's primary role was to measure topography and to provide a high-accuracy reference frame for other LRO data [1][3]. The LOLA paper reports a mean lunar radius and shape parameters derived from its measurements [1].
- Polar illumination and permanently shadowed regions. The LRO objectives for LOLA include characterising polar illumination and imaging permanently shadowed regions [3][1].
- Surface slope, roughness and reflectance. LOLA produces products for slopes, roughness and surface brightness at 1064 nm [3][1].
- Global topographic mapping by earlier missions. Clementine lidar profiles were used to construct the first global topographic map of the Moon [6]. KAGUYA's LALT was intended to construct a global, accurate and precise topographic map of the Moon [5]. A later study reports a lunar digital elevation model built from Chang'e-1 LAM data [8]; that paper was not accessed in full.
- Support for imaging. The Clementine lidar also produced high-resolution colour images, so its laser and camera functions were combined [6].
article.operating_principle: The basic relation is range = (speed of light x round-trip time) / 2. For a spacecraft at 50 km altitude, the round trip for a pulse is roughly 333 microseconds, which shows why the timing electronics must be precise. LOLA's time-of-flight measurement is paired with a stated range precision of about 10 cm on a flat surface, limited by pulse energy, receiver aperture and spacecraft altitude [1]. The returned pulse also widens when it hits rough terrain, and the width is recorded as a roughness indicator [1][3]. The laser wavelength matters. LOLA uses 1064 nm for mapping. It also has a 532 nm laser path that was used for laser ranging from Earth stations to LRO [1][2]. Orbital altimeters also need accurate knowledge of where the laser points relative to the spacecraft. After launch, LOLA's laser boresight vector was measured in experiments in which LRO pointed away from the Moon and scanned the Earth in a raster pattern while the laser fired [1].
article.scientific_importance: A laser altimeter gives direct height measurements that do not depend on lighting, so it can measure terrain that cameras find hard to interpret. The LOLA paper describes its dataset as one of the foundational datasets of the LRO mission and reports a geodetic frame and topography used to find permanently shadowed regions at the lunar poles [1]. The Clementine lidar produced topographic profiles from which the first global topographic map of the Moon was constructed [6]. JAXA states that LALT ranging data were intended to build a global, accurate and precise topographic map of the Moon [5].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a laser altimeter. The examples below differ in mission, orbit, laser energy, beam configuration, receiver size and documentation type. Each value is tied to a named instrument and source. Where a source does not publish a value, the table says "not publicly specified". Values are not ranked, and the table compares only parameters that the sources state for more than one example.

examples.name: Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) on Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
examples.status: Flown. LRO was launched on 18 June 2009, and LOLA has operated nearly continuously since 3 July 2009 [1]. The 2016 paper describes the instrument as still mapping in 2016 [1]. Operations after 2016 were not verified in this run.
examples.published_configuration: The NASA pre-launch fact sheet gives a mass of 9.6 kg; a volume of 0.45 m long, 0.31 m wide and 0.35 m high; a power of 26.2 W average with a 29.9 W turn-on peak; a data rate of 10 kbps; and a link margin of 5.4 dB at 50 km [3]. It gives a laser of 1064 nm, 2.4 mJ per pulse at 28 Hz, a 14 cm receiver aperture, a 100 microradian beam divergence, five beams separated by 500 microradians, and a +/-10 cm altimeter measurement [3]. The optics paper gives a 140 mm receiver clear aperture and a required output energy of 2.7 mJ [2]. The 2016 in-flight paper gives a laser pulse rate of 28 Hz, a pulse width of 5 ns in its Table 1, a 1064.4 +/-0.1 nm wavelength, a range precision of about 10 cm on a flat surface, and a 50 km mapping orbit with 57 m along-track sample spacing [1].
examples.evidence_limits: The mass and power values are pre-launch values from the fact sheet [3]. A secondary source gives 11.3 kg and 33.4 W [10]; the conflict is not resolved here. The pulse energy differs between the fact sheet (2.4 mJ) and the optics paper text (2.7 mJ) [3][2]. The pre-launch optics table lists 2.7 ns for pulse width, while the 2016 flight table lists 5 ns [2][1]. The figure shown for this example is a LOLA-derived elevation rendering, not a hardware image, and no LOLA hardware photograph with a verified direct URL was found in this run.

examples.name: Laser Altimeter (LALT) on KAGUYA (SELENE)
examples.status: Flown. JAXA's LALT page describes LALT as one of the instruments on the KAGUYA main orbiter [5]. The JAXA page does not state the instrument's operating dates, so the mission timing was not verified from a primary source in this run.
examples.published_configuration: JAXA lists a wavelength of 1064 nm, a laser output energy of 100 mJ, a pulse repetition rate of 1 Hz, a mass of 20 kg, and ranging accuracy of 5 m. It gives a measurement range of 50 to 150 km [5]. It lists two dimension sets: LALT-TR at 306 x 450 x 408 mm and LALT-E at 301 x 241 x 88 mm [5]. The page does not list a power value or a height-resolution value [5]. The stated purpose is to produce a global, accurate and precise topographic map of the Moon [5].
examples.evidence_limits: The 5 m figure is JAXA's stated ranging accuracy [5]. Conference abstracts reported in a search summary give 1 m, which was not verified and is not used. LALT-TR and LALT-E are listed as separate dimension sets; the page does not explain how they relate to the flight configuration, so no single flight envelope is given. The illustration and track map shown here are JAXA images; the map shows altimetry points over a region of the Moon as an example of coverage, not a site recommendation.

examples.name: Lunar Laser Ranging Instrument (LLRI) on Chandrayaan-1
examples.type: Flown lunar orbiter laser ranging instrument
examples.status: Flown as a payload of the Chandrayaan-1 orbiter, as ISRO's Chandrayaan-1 payload page describes it [9]. The launch and end-of-mission dates were not re-verified in this run because the ISSDC mission page was not reachable. In-flight LLRI performance was not verified.
examples.published_configuration: ISRO describes an Nd:YAG laser at 1064 nm, with 10 mJ per pulse and a 10 Hz pulse repetition mode [9]. The returning pulse is collected by a 200 mm Ritchey-Chretien optical receiver and detected by a silicon avalanche photodetector [9]. The mass is given as 11.37 kg with base plate [9]. The power is not stated [9]. The stated objective is to provide ranging data for determining the height difference between the spacecraft and the lunar surface, which ISRO describes as yielding highly accurate range and spot elevation measurements [9]. The page does not use the word altimeter for LLRI.
examples.evidence_limits: A research paper reported in a search summary describes a different receiver design, a two-mirror Zerodur Zall-Kirkham receiver, and a single avalanche photodiode [search summary; paper not accessed]. The two descriptions conflict, and this article uses the ISRO page's values with that caveat. No accuracy figure for LLRI was verified.

examples.name: Clementine imaging lidar, altimetry mode
examples.type: Flown lunar orbiter lidar with laser altimetry mode
examples.status: Flown. Clementine was launched on 25 January 1994 on a Titan II booster and reached lunar orbit after a phasing sequence [6]. The mission paper describes the lidar as operating as a laser altimeter when the spacecraft was closer than 640 km to the Moon [6].
examples.published_configuration: The lidar made topographic profiles by taking spot ranging measurements of about 100 m, with precision of about 50 m, at intervals of about 2 km along track [6]. Adjacent orbital profiles were spaced by about 2.5 degrees of longitude, or about 70 km at the chosen perilune latitudes of +/-30 degrees [6]. Altimetry was reported for latitudes from 70 degrees north to 70 degrees south [6]. The same instrument also produced high-resolution colour images, typically about 20 m per pixel, in up to four colours [6]. The spacecraft mass was 140 kg [6]; no separate lidar mass, power or dimensions were given in the accessed text.
examples.evidence_limits: The lidar's laser wavelength, mass, power and dimensions were not found in the accessed mission paper [6]. The paper's latitude coverage is used here; a search summary gave 75 degrees, which was not used. The publication date of the NASA technical memorandum record was not verified. The 140 kg figure is for the spacecraft, not the lidar.

examples.name: Laser altimeter (LAM) on Chang'e-1
examples.status: Flown. The eoPortal Chang'e-1 page gives a launch date of 24 October 2007 [7]. It states that the mission officially ended in October 2008 and that the spacecraft was guided to impact on 1 March 2009 [7]. The page's quick-facts end-of-life date (3 January 2009) does not match the impact date, so the end date is recorded as inconsistent.
examples.published_configuration: The eoPortal page gives a laser wavelength of 1064 nm, a laser energy of 150 mJ per pulse, a spot size below 120 m, a range uncertainty of 5 m or less, and a range resolution of 1 m or less [7]. It gives a telescope aperture of 140 mm, a Cassegrain-type receiver and a silicon avalanche photodiode detector [7]. The stated lunar operating altitude is 200 km with a tolerance of +/-25 km [7]. The page states that the orbit was lowered to 100 km in December 2008 [7].
examples.evidence_limits: The eoPortal page does not state a pulse repetition rate or pulse width for LAM [7]. A search summary gave 5 to 7 ns and one measurement per second, which were not verified. Because of the December 2008 orbit change, the 200 km altitude does not apply to the whole mission [7]. DEM accuracy figures reported in search summaries [8] are not used here and were not checked against full text.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are reported only for named units. LOLA: 0.45 m x 0.31 m x 0.35 m pre-launch [3]. KAGUYA LALT: LALT-TR 306 x 450 x 408 mm and LALT-E 301 x 241 x 88 mm [5]. Clementine, LLRI and Chang'e-1 dimensions were not publicly specified in the accessed sources. These values are not a general altimeter envelope.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: LOLA pre-launch mass 9.6 kg [3], with a conflicting secondary value of 11.3 kg [10] not used. KAGUYA LALT 20 kg [5]. LLRI 11.37 kg with base plate [9]. Clementine spacecraft mass 140 kg, with no separate lidar mass [6]. Chang'e-1 LAM mass not publicly specified in the accessed source [7].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LOLA 26.2 W average, 29.9 W turn-on peak, pre-launch [3]. KAGUYA LALT: not listed [5]. LLRI: not stated [9]. Clementine lidar: not stated [6]. Chang'e-1 LAM: not publicly specified in the accessed source [7].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar laser altimeter operates in vacuum with large thermal swings. The LOLA optical transceiver is mounted on the LRO instrument deck, is fully enclosed by thermal blankets, and uses titanium flexures to isolate it from structural loads [2]. The receiver objective lens material was compared on predicted on-orbit temperatures before selection [2]. Ranging accuracy depends on pulse energy, the receiver aperture and the spacecraft altitude, so altitude changes affect precision [1]. Data rates and power are also constraints. LOLA's data rate is 10 kbps and its power is 26.2 W average, with a 29.9 W turn-on peak, according to the pre-launch fact sheet [3]. Spacecraft position and attitude must be known to convert ranges to surface heights, so altimeters depend on the spacecraft navigation system [1].
article.limitations: A laser altimeter measures range to the first surface that returns enough light. It does not identify materials by itself. Its precision depends on pulse energy, receiver aperture, altitude and surface reflectance; LOLA's ranging precision of about 10 cm applies to a flat surface, not to steep or rough terrain [1]. Weak returns are a limit: the LOLA paper notes that automatic noise rejection can be imperfect when the return rate is low [1]. Orbital altimetry gives height along narrow ground tracks, so global coverage requires many orbits. Chang'e-1's LAM operated at a nominal 200 km altitude, while LOLA's mapping orbit was 50 km, so their profiles are not directly interchangeable [7][1]. Specifications in this article come from pre-launch documents for some instruments and from flight-operations papers for others. They should not be combined.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: All five examples are orbital instruments. Their relevant interfaces are spacecraft integration, mounting and alignment, thermal control, pointing knowledge, power and data handling, launch, lunar transfer, orbit insertion and commissioning. LOLA's pointing calibration was part of integration, and the instrument was aligned so that its centre laser beam and receiver field of view were within the boresight tolerance set in the optical requirements [2]. After launch, LOLA's boresight vector was measured using Earth scans with the laser firing [1].
transportation_process: Integrate the altimeter and its optical transceiver onto the spacecraft's instrument deck, with alignment checks and thermal blanketing [2].
Launch the spacecraft on a launch vehicle. LOLA was carried on LRO, which launched on 18 June 2009 [1].
Transfer to the Moon and enter a commissioning orbit. LRO's commissioning orbit had a periapsis of about 30 km above the south pole [1].
Enter the mapping orbit. LRO reached a near-circular 50 km mapping orbit on 27 September 2009, three months after entering commissioning [1].
Commission the instrument and calibrate boresight using Earth scans [1].
Operate the altimeter during the mission. LRO's orbit was later changed, with the periapsis band reported as 30 to 200 km from December 2011 and 20 to 40 km from spring 2015 [1].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Orbital altimeters are not deployed on the surface. Their pointing is set by the spacecraft attitude control system and by a fixed mount. A surface altimeter, if one is used on a lander, would need its own mounting, pointing and calibration, but no lander-mounted example with verified specifications was found in this run.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LOLA flew on LRO from 2009, with nearly continuous operation from 3 July 2009 through the period covered by the 2016 paper [1]. KAGUYA's LALT flew on the KAGUYA main orbiter [5]. LLRI was a payload on Chandrayaan-1 [9]. Clementine was launched on a Titan II booster from Vandenberg on 25 January 1994 and used a kick motor and phasing orbits to reach lunar orbit [6]. Chang'e-1 was launched on 24 October 2007 [7].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted in this article. Such an assertion would require verified interface documents for the named vehicle. A future altimeter's requirements would be set by its mass, dimensions, power, data interface, mounting points, pointing accuracy and thermal limits, which would need to be compared with verified spacecraft specifications.

article.historical_significance: The Clementine mission (1994) used lidar altimetry profiles from which the first global topographic map of the Moon was constructed [6]. LOLA, launched in 2009, acquired nearly 7 billion altimetric measurements by March 2016 and provides a geodetic reference for other LRO data [1]. KAGUYA's LALT, the Chang'e-1 LAM and Chandrayaan-1's LLRI added altimetry and ranging instruments from other national programmes [5][7][9].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- LOLA pre-launch versus flight values. The LOLA fact sheet is a pre-launch document that gives 9.6 kg and 26.2 W [3]. A secondary source reports 11.3 kg and 33.4 W [10]. This conflict was not resolved from a primary flight document, so no mass or power value is used as a flight measurement in this article.
- LOLA pulse energy and width. The fact sheet gives 2.4 mJ per pulse [3], while the optics paper text describes a required 2.7 mJ output energy [2]. The pre-launch optics table, as read from its text-extracted layout, appears to give a pulse width of 2.7 ns, while the 2016 in-flight table gives 5 ns [2][1]. These differences were not reconciled.
- LOLA operational status. The most recent primary paper accessed describes operations to 2016 [1]. Operating status after that date was not verified.
- KAGUYA LALT accuracy and power. JAXA gives ranging accuracy as 5 m [5]. Secondary search summaries cited 1 m in conference abstracts, but those were not verified. JAXA does not publish a power value or a height-resolution value for LALT [5].
- LLRI receiver optics. The ISRO page describes a 200 mm Ritchey-Chretien receiver and a silicon avalanche photodetector [9]. A research paper reported in a search summary describes a different receiver design, but the paper was not accessed, so the conflict is unresolved. LLRI power is not stated [9].
- Clementine lidar. The accessed mission paper gives the spot size, precision, spacing and coverage, but not the lidar laser wavelength, mass, power or dimensions [6]. The coverage was stated as 70 degrees north to 70 degrees south in that paper; a search summary gave 75 degrees, which was not used.
- Chang'e-1 LAM. The eoPortal page gives the laser energy, altitude, spot size and range uncertainty [7]. It does not give a pulse rate. Its mission dates are inconsistent, and the operating altitude was lowered to 100 km in December 2008 [7]. Chang'e-1 DEM accuracy figures reported in search summaries [8] were not verified against full text and are not used numerically.
- Chandrayaan-3 lander altimeter. ISRO's listing of a laser altimeter for the Chandrayaan-3 lander was reported in a search summary, but the ISRO page was not accessible in this run. No specifications were verified, so the instrument is not profiled.
- Images. The JAXA image img_lalt_005 is a portrait of a person and was excluded. Copyright and reuse conditions for the JAXA and NASA images were not checked, and full-resolution downloads were not checked.

references.title: Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL) NASA technical paper (adjacent sensor; not profiled)
references.notes: Search summary only; not accessed in full. Cited only for the adjacency note in the Overview.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values, and all reference URLs, have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. Each image was checked to return HTTP 200 with its clean URL. The JAXA LALT image pages were read with WebFetch, and the image assets were fetched directly.

data_quality_notes: LOLA mass and power conflict: the NASA pre-launch fact sheet gives 9.6 kg and 26.2 W [3]; a secondary source gives 11.3 kg and 33.4 W [10]. No primary flight value was verified, so neither is presented as a flight measurement.

LOLA pulse energy and width: the fact sheet gives 2.4 mJ [3]; the optics paper text gives a required 2.7 mJ [2]. The pre-launch optics table gives a pulse width of 2.7 ns, and the 2016 in-flight Table 1 gives 5 ns [1][2]. These were not reconciled.
LOLA operating status after 2016 was not verified; the most recent primary paper accessed is the 2016 Icarus summary [1].

KAGUYA LALT: JAXA gives 5 m ranging accuracy [5]; a search summary cited 1 m from conference abstracts, which was not verified. JAXA gives no power or height-resolution value and no operating dates on the LALT page [5]. The two LALT dimension sets are not identified with a flown configuration.

LLRI: the ISRO page gives a 200 mm Ritchey-Chretien receiver and silicon avalanche photodetector [9]. A research paper reported in a search summary describes a different receiver design; the paper was not accessed. LLRI power is not stated and no accuracy value was verified. The ISSDC mission page was not reachable, so the launch and end dates were not re-verified.

Clementine lidar: the accessed NASA mission paper gives spot size, precision, spacing, altimetry range and latitude coverage (70 degrees), but not the lidar wavelength, mass, power or dimensions [6]. A search summary gave 75 degrees, which was not used. The publication date of the NTRS record was not verified.

Chang'e-1 LAM: eoPortal gives laser energy, altitude, spot and range uncertainty but no pulse rate or pulse width [7]. The eoPortal mission dates are internally inconsistent (quick-facts end of life 3 January 2009; impact 1 March 2009; official end October 2008) [7]. The 200 km altitude does not apply after the December 2008 lowering to 100 km [7].

Chang'e-1 DEM: the Huang et al. (2018) Advances in Astronomy paper [8] was not accessed in full (the publisher page returned HTTP 403). A 3.52 m ranging figure from an MDPI review was also not accessed (HTTP 403) and is not used. Accuracy figures from search summaries are not used numerically.

Chandrayaan-3 laser altimeter: ISRO's listing was reported in a search summary, but the ISRO Chandrayaan-3 page returned HTTP 404 in this run. No specifications were verified, so the instrument is not profiled as an example.

Adjacent sensor: the NASA Navigation Doppler Lidar flown on IM-1 [11] is a lidar ranging and velocity sensor for navigation. It was identified through a search summary only and is not profiled; the 046 and 048 entries cover the adjacent lidar and rangefinder classes.

Image rights: the NASA SVS image and JAXA LALT images were checked for HTTP 200 and their source pages were read, but their reuse terms and full-resolution downloads were not checked. The JAXA img_lalt_005 image is a portrait of a person and was excluded. No image of LOLA hardware was verified; the NASA image is a data visualization.
Transportation compatibility: no lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted. transportation_compatibility_verified_for_specific_landers is false.
Spaceflight Now [10] and the Icarus DOI page were read only through search summaries or not at all; they are listed for transparency and the DOI is given in the reference notes only.
